core: Working definition of prenatal development: the growth and change of a human being from conception to birth
The three periods of prenatal development: germinal, embryonic, fetal, one factual line each
The placenta as the lifeline between parent and fetus
Teratogens: alcohol, tobacco, and some infections, named factually as risks per CDC/NICHD, no scare content
Prenatal care: monitoring and nutrition, stated factually, no advice
Honest note: most pregnancies end with healthy babies
Honest framing: prenatal life is the fastest development a person ever does
supporting: Zygote, embryo, and fetus as the terms for the developing human at each stage
Trimesters as a calendar division of pregnancy, distinct from developmental periods
Congenital disorders (~3% of U.S. births) as the baseline for the honest note
outOfScope: Embryology in depth (owned by the biology subject)
Clinical prenatal care practice and procedures (owned by the nursing subject)
Postnatal development, infancy, and later life stages (own sibling topics)

claims.claim: Prenatal development is the growth and change of a human being from conception to birth; it unfolds in three major periods, the germinal, the embryonic, and the fetal.
The germinal period runs from conception to about two weeks: the single cell formed at conception (the zygote) divides, travels to the uterus, and implants there.

The embryonic period runs from the third through the eighth week of pregnancy, a period of enormous change in which the embryo forms its major body structures and its support systems, including the placenta.
The fetal period runs from about the ninth week to birth: the fetus grows quickly while organs grow and refine, and during this last period the fetus becomes viable outside the womb.

The placenta is a temporary organ connecting the uterus to the umbilical cord that provides respiration and nourishment for the embryo and fetus and eliminates waste: the lifeline between parent and fetus.

A teratogen is any disease, drug, or other environmental agent that can harm the embryo or the fetus physically or influence health or behavior after birth; the key word is 'can', so teratogens raise risk rather than guarantee harm.

Alcohol: CDC reports that alcohol use during pregnancy is associated with an increased risk of miscarriage, preterm birth, stillbirth, and sudden infant death syndrome, and can cause a range of lifelong behavioral, intellectual, and physical disabilities known as fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASDs); there is no known safe amount, and not all babies exposed will be affected.

Tobacco: CDC reports that smoking during pregnancy can cause a baby to be born too early or to have low birth weight, and smoking during and after pregnancy is a risk factor for sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).
Some infections: NICHD reports that infections such as rubella, cytomegalovirus (CMV), Zika, and toxoplasmosis can affect a pregnancy and harm the developing fetus.

Prenatal care is the health care a person gets while pregnant, including regular checkups and monitoring, and it helps keep the pregnant person and the fetus healthy and lets providers spot problems early; people who do not receive regular prenatal care are at higher risk of having a baby with low birth weight.

Honest note: most pregnancies end with a healthy baby; approximately 3 percent of infants born in the United States have a congenital disorder, and a healthy pregnancy is never guaranteed though prenatal behaviors and choices can improve the odds.

Honest framing: prenatal life is the fastest development a person ever does, from a single cell at conception to a fetus with functioning organ systems in about nine months; the germinal period is the shortest of the three, the embryonic period brings enormous change, and the fetal period is one of rapid growth.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Do teratogen exposures guarantee harm to the baby?
positions: Popular accounts sometimes imply that any exposure to alcohol, tobacco, or an infection during pregnancy causes a birth defect.
CDC states that not all babies will be affected by alcohol during pregnancy and that it is impossible to know which babies will be affected.

OpenStax defines a teratogen as an agent that can harm the embryo or fetus, and its healthy-pregnancy section states that a healthy pregnancy is never guaranteed while behaviors and choices can improve the odds.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states teratogen effects as risks, never as certainties, matching the CDC's 'not all babies will be affected' note and OpenStax's 'can harm' definition, with no scare language.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is the germinal period counted from conception or from the last menstrual period?
positions: OpenStax Lifespan Development counts the germinal period from conception, lasting about two weeks.
NICHD measures pregnancy itself as about 40 weeks from the last menstrual period to delivery, and describes the first trimester as weeks 1-12.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows OpenStax for the developmental periods (germinal from conception) and presents NICHD's 40-week trimester calendar only as the separate calendar framework, avoiding any conflation of the two counting systems.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's boilerplate ('Prenatal Development is a foundational concept in Human Development. This lesson introduces its meaning, its context, and a simple way to apply it.') contains no factual content and was discarded entirely.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated boilerplate draft with original prose; no draft wording was retained.
Teratogen examples (alcohol, tobacco, infections) are stated as risks per CDC/NICHD, not as guarantees of harm, per the source-map caution against scare content.
Prenatal care is described factually (monitoring and nutrition) with no medical advice, per scope.
Embryology detail and birth were kept out of scope; the lesson points to sibling topics instead.

sourceRecords.title: OpenStax Lifespan Development, Section 2.3: Pregnancy and Prenatal Development (Chapter 2: Genetic, Prenatal, and Perinatal Health)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook. Canonical openstax.org URL registered; openstax.org blocks direct fetch, so the section was read via Wayback Machine capture 20260520093353 of the canonical URL. Supports: the three major developmental periods of pregnancy (germinal, embryonic, fetal); the germinal period from conception to about two weeks (zygote, blastocyst, implantation, the life-support system of placenta, umbilical cord, amnion, and chorion); the embryonic period from the third to the eighth week with the placenta defined as a temporary organ connecting the uterus to the umbilical cord providing respiration and nourishment and eliminating waste; the fetal period as the last seven months of organ growth and refinement with rapid growth and viability; the teratogen definition (any disease, drug, or other environmental agent that can harm the embryo or fetus); the teratogen impact table citing CDC (alcohol, nicotine, infections such as rubella and CMV); the healthy-pregnancy section (regular prenatal care associated with lower low-birth-weight risk; a healthy pregnancy is never guaranteed but behaviors and choices improve the odds); approximately 3 percent of U.S. infants born with a congenital disorder (citing CDC). Facts synthesized in original prose; no textbook wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: About Pregnancy (NICHD)
sourceRecords.provider: Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD), NIH
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: pregnancy as the period in which a fetus develops inside the womb, usually lasting about 40 weeks or just over 9 months as measured from the last menstrual period; the three trimesters (first: week 1-12, beginning with conception, the fertilized egg called a zygote traveling to the uterus and implanting; second: week 13-28; third: week 29-40); infants born before 37 weeks considered preterm; the zygote-embryo-fetus terminology as the developing human advances. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What infections can affect pregnancy? (NICHD, About Pregnancy)
sourceRecords.provider: Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD), NIH
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: infections that can affect pregnancy and harm the developing fetus, named factually — rubella (German measles) can cause problems with the pregnancy and congenital anomalies in the infant; cytomegalovirus (CMV), a common virus, can be passed to the fetus; Zika infection during pregnancy can cause pregnancy loss, other pregnancy complications, and congenital defects; toxoplasmosis, caused by a parasite, can pass from a pregnant person to the developing fetus. Used only for the one-line-per-infection risk statements; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: About Alcohol Use During Pregnancy (CDC)
sourceRecords.provider: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Canonical cdc.gov URL registered; cdc.gov blocks direct fetch, so the page was read via Wayback Machine capture 20240716024231 of the canonical URL (page dated May 15, 2024). Supports: alcohol use during pregnancy is associated with an increased risk of miscarriage, preterm birth, stillbirth, and sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS); alcohol use during pregnancy can cause a range of lifelong behavioral, intellectual, and physical disabilities known as fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASDs); during pregnancy alcohol can pass from the pregnant person to the fetus and affect its development; there is no known safe amount of alcohol and no safe time during pregnancy; not all babies will be affected by alcohol during pregnancy, and it is impossible to know which babies will be affected. Risk language only, stated factually; no wording reproduced.
